# Introduction

- Structural equation modeling (SEM) is used to study relationships among multiple variables. It can include observed variables, which are directly measured, and latent variables, which cannot be measured directly.

- SEM combines factor analysis and regression and can also account for measurement error.

- Anderson and Gerbing focus on SEM for theory testing and development. They divide SEM into two parts: the measurement model and the structural model. The measurement model looks at how observed indicators relate to latent constructs, while the structural model looks at relationships among the latent constructs.

- The authors recommend evaluating the measurement model first and then testing the structural model [@anderson1988, 411].

# Background

## Exploratory Versus Confirmatory Analyses

- Exploratory and confirmatory analyses are not completely separate. The authors describe them more as a progression [@anderson1988, 412].

- In exploratory analysis, researchers may not know the factor structure in advance.

- In confirmatory analysis, the measurement model is specified a priori, before the parameters are estimated.

- If researchers change the model after looking at the results, the analysis becomes partly exploratory.

- A modified model should ideally be cross-validated with a different sample [@anderson1988, 412].

## Complementary Approaches for Theory Testing Versus Predictive Application

- Anderson and Gerbing distinguish between SEM used for theory testing and SEM used for prediction.

- Maximum likelihood (ML) and generalized least squares (GLS) are more focused on theory testing. They separate measurement error from the latent construct and provide an overall model-fit test.

- Partial least squares (PLS) is more prediction oriented. In the approach discussed in the article, it focuses more on explaining variance.

- PLS does not provide the same assessment of unidimensionality or an overall model-fit test [@anderson1988, 412].

## Estimation Methods

- Maximum likelihood was the most commonly used estimation method for covariance-based SEM.

- ML assumes multivariate normality and has useful large-sample properties.

- Moderate nonnormality may not strongly affect the parameter estimates, but it can affect the standard errors and chi-square test [@anderson1988, 413].

- The article also discusses other methods such as GLS and asymptotically distribution-free (ADF) estimation.

- ADF makes fewer distributional assumptions, but it usually needs a larger sample and more computation.

# Confirmatory Measurement Model

- A confirmatory measurement model shows how observed indicators relate to their latent constructs.

- At this stage, the latent constructs are allowed to correlate freely.

- The main goal is to make sure the constructs are being measured properly before testing structural relationships.

## Need for Unidimensional Measurement

- Unidimensionality means that a set of indicators mainly measures one underlying construct.

- It is important because researchers need a clear meaning for each latent construct.

- Anderson and Gerbing discuss internal consistency and external consistency as two ways to assess unidimensionality [@anderson1988, 414].

- They prefer multiple indicators because they help define the construct more clearly.

- Cross-loadings or correlated measurement errors can make the meaning of a construct less clear [@anderson1988, 415].

## Specification

- Because latent variables are not directly observed, their scale needs to be set.

- Anderson and Gerbing prefer fixing the factor variance to 1.0 instead of fixing one factor loading to 1.0 [@anderson1988, 415].

- This allows all factor loadings to be tested for significance.

- Multiple indicators are preferred, but sometimes only one indicator is available.

- With a single indicator, researchers need an estimate of measurement error, ideally from previous research.

### Sample Size

- Sample size matters because SEM depends on large-sample statistical properties.

- A sample size of around 150 or more was found to be useful for getting stable estimates [@anderson1988, 415].

- For models with three or more indicators per factor, around 150 observations will usually give a converged and proper solution [@anderson1988, 416].

- Models with only two indicators per factor may need a larger sample.

- Small samples can increase the chance of nonconvergence or improper solutions.

- Some distribution-free methods may need around 400 to 500 observations or more [@anderson1988, 416].

## Assessment of Fit

- After the measurement model converges, researchers check how well it fits the data.

- The article discusses the chi-square test, goodness-of-fit index, root-mean-square residual, and normed and nonnormed fit indices [@anderson1988, 416].

- Model fit is important, but researchers also need to check construct validity.

### Convergent Validity

- Convergent validity means that indicators of the same construct should relate well to that construct.

- Anderson and Gerbing suggest checking whether each factor loading is statistically significant.

- A loading is considered significant when it is greater than about twice its standard error [@anderson1988, 416].

### Discriminant Validity

- Discriminant validity means that two different constructs should be distinguishable from each other.

- The authors suggest testing one pair of constructs at a time.

- One method is to fix their correlation at 1.0 and compare that model with the unconstrained model using a chi-square difference test [@anderson1988, 416].

- Researchers can also check whether the confidence interval around the correlation includes 1.0 [@anderson1988, 416].

## Respecification

- Sometimes the first measurement model does not fit well, so some respecification may be needed.

- The authors emphasize that changes should be based on both theory and statistical results [@anderson1988, 416].

- Possible changes include:

  - moving an indicator to another factor;
  - deleting an indicator;
  - allowing an indicator to load on more than one factor; or
  - allowing correlated measurement errors.

- The first two options are usually preferred because they are more likely to preserve unidimensionality [@anderson1988, 417].

- Cross-loadings and correlated errors may improve fit, but they can also make the constructs harder to interpret.

- Residuals can also help find possible model problems [@anderson1988, 417].

# One-Step Versus Two-Step Modeling Approaches

## The Confirmatory Structural Model

- The structural model focuses on relationships among latent constructs.

- It can include exogenous constructs, whose causes are outside the model, and endogenous constructs, whose causes are included in the model [@anderson1988, 418].

- The measurement and structural parts can be estimated at the same time, but this can make it harder to see where a problem comes from.

### Interpretational Confounding

- One problem with the one-step approach is interpretational confounding.

- This happens when the meaning of a latent construct changes depending on how the structural model is specified.

- One sign is that factor loadings change a lot across different structural models.

- Evaluating the measurement model first helps reduce this problem [@anderson1988, 418].

## Recommended Two-Step Modeling Approach

### Step 1: Evaluate the Measurement Model

- The first step is to estimate the measurement model using confirmatory factor analysis.

- The indicators are linked to their expected latent constructs, and the latent constructs are allowed to correlate freely.

- Researchers mainly check:

  - unidimensionality;
  - overall model fit;
  - factor loadings;
  - convergent validity; and
  - discriminant validity.

- If the measurement model does not fit well, researchers should fix the measurement problem before moving to the structural model.

### Step 2: Evaluate the Structural Model

- After an acceptable measurement model is established, researchers move to the structural model.

- The structural model tests the hypothesized relationships among latent constructs.

- The difference is simple:

  - the measurement model asks whether the indicators measure the constructs well;
  - the structural model asks whether the constructs relate to each other as expected.

- This step also helps assess nomological validity, or whether the constructs relate to other constructs in theoretically expected ways [@anderson1988, 411].

## Nested Models and Sequential Chi-Square Difference Tests

- Anderson and Gerbing recommend comparing five nested structural models [@anderson1988, 418–419]:

  1.  $M_s$: saturated model;
  2.  $M_n$: null model;
  3.  $M_t$: theoretical model;
  4.  $M_c$: more constrained alternative;
  5.  $M_u$: less constrained alternative.

- The models follow this order: $M_n$ \< $M_c$ \< $M_t$ \< $M_u$ \< $M_s$

- The authors use sequential chi-square difference tests (SCDTs) to compare these models.

- This helps researchers compare the main theoretical model with both more restricted and less restricted alternatives [@anderson1988, 418–420].

## Advantages of the Two-Step Approach

- The two-step approach helps separate measurement problems from structural problems.

- It also prevents good fit in one part of the model from hiding poor fit in another part.

- Evaluating measurement first helps reduce interpretational confounding.

- It also makes it easier to compare alternative theoretical models [@anderson1988, 421–422].

## Additional Considerations in Structural Model Interpretation

### Statistical Versus Practical Significance

- Chi-square tests are affected by sample size.

- With a large sample, even a small model difference can become statistically significant.

- Because of this, researchers should also look at practical fit measures such as the normed fit index (NFI) [@anderson1988, 421].

### Cautions About Causal Interpretation

- Good model fit does not prove that one construct causes another.

- A good fit only shows that the data are consistent with the proposed model.

- Other models may also explain the same data.

- Model modification can also make causal conclusions weaker, so cross-validation with another sample is useful when possible.

# Conclusion

- Anderson and Gerbing recommend evaluating the measurement model before testing the structural model.

- The first step focuses on measurement quality, especially unidimensionality, convergent validity, and discriminant validity.

- The second step focuses on theoretical relationships among latent constructs and nomological validity.

- The two-step approach makes it easier to see whether a problem comes from measurement or from the structural model.

- The main takeaway is that good SEM analysis needs both good measurement and strong theoretical support.

# References

Anderson, James C., and David W. Gerbing. 1988. “Structural Equation Modeling in Practice: A Review and Recommended Two-Step Approach.” *Psychological Bulletin* 103 (3): 411–423. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.103.3.411.
